one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban addresses whether the SC can reverse Senate rulings and stop Corona's impeachment. The Senate denied Corona's motion for a preliminary hearing (on claims of improper verification and lack of notice/hearing). The general rule: No -- the three great branches are co-equal; the House has the exclusive power to initiate and the Senate has the sole power to try and decide; it would be self-serving for impeached justices to use the SC to reverse proceedings against themselves. The exception: Francisco v. House of Representatives (November 10, 2003) held that the SC has the constitutional duty (not power -- and per CJ Concepcion, a duty 'cannot under any circumstance be evaded') to check any branch for grave abuse of discretion (arbitrary, whimsical, capricious, or despotic exercise arising from passion or personal hostility). The question left to 'citizen-judges' (the readers): did the Senate commit GAD in denying the preliminary hearing? Five private citizens have already petitioned the SC on the same grounds, but Corona himself is not a petitioner. If he does not file his own certiorari, the five petitions would be 'orphaned' -- and the SC may ask why it should grant relief when the person most interested in the outcome has abstained. The column closes by defending the 'more political than legal' formulation against an IBP officer's charge of 'championing mob rule' -- political means policy, not mob rule.
